title: THE DRY TOWN
lines: To understand how this happened, you have to understand Lahaina.
For a time in the 1800s, this small town on the west coast of Maui was the royal capital of the Kingdom of Hawaiʻi.
King Kamehameha the Third lived here, on a tiny island in the middle of a spring-fed pond called Mokuhinia.
Lahaina was a place of water. Streams ran down from the mountains, through taro fields and fishponds, to the sea.
Then came the whaling ships. And after them, sugar.
Plantations diverted the mountain streams to water their cane. The royal pond dried up. In 1919, it was filled in and turned into a baseball field.
By the twenty-first century, Lahaina was one of the driest places in Hawaiʻi, with about fifteen inches of rain a year.
Front Street ran along the ocean, lined with wooden buildings from the whaling days. In the town square stood a banyan tree, planted in 1873, that had grown to cover almost an acre.
And on the hills above the town, something else was growing.
When the plantations closed, the fields were left empty. African grasses, brought in to feed cattle, took over. Guinea grass. Buffel grass. Molasses grass.
Guinea grass can grow six inches in a single day. When it dries out, it burns with flames up to twenty feet high.
By 2023, Lahaina was a historic wooden town, surrounded on three sides by fuel.

title: THE WARNINGS
lines: None of this was a secret.
In 2014, a wildfire protection plan for West Maui was signed. News reports say it rated Lahaina's fire risk as extreme.
In August 2018, as Hurricane Lane approached, a fire broke out in the Kauaʻula Valley, just south of town. It burned fifteen hundred acres and damaged or destroyed twenty-one homes.
A deputy fire chief called the conditions unprecedented in the department's history.
Years later, investigators found something striking. The fire department and the police never even started a formal review of the 2018 fire. The emergency agency never finished one.
Far to the south, Hurricane Dora was passing the islands at a safe distance. To the north sat a strong high-pressure system. Between them, the air was squeezed into a powerful river of wind.
On August seventh, the National Weather Service issued a red flag warning. Its wind warnings said the gusts could blow down trees and power lines.
The next day, gusts reached eighty miles an hour.

title: THE MORNING
lines: Just after 6:30 in the morning on August eighth, the wind brought down power lines near Lahainaluna Road, on the upper edge of town.
A resident named Shane Treu called 911. The lines had sparked the dry grass.
Firefighters fought the blaze for hours in the wind. By around nine, it was declared contained.
At about 2:18 in the afternoon, after nearly eight hours on scene, the crews left. The fire chief would later say it had been fully contained and extinguished.
Thirty-four minutes later, it was burning again.
Shortly before three, a Hawaiian Electric crew working nearby saw a small fire, and called 911.
Federal investigators would call it a rekindle. Something in the morning burn area was still alive.
A spark carried by the wind. Smoldering material moved by heavy equipment. Or a root, burning slowly underground.
Even after a year of work, investigators could not rule out any of the three.

title: THE AFTERNOON
lines: This time, nothing could stop it.
The fire jumped the Lahaina Bypass. Around 3:30, the first homes on Lahainaluna Road caught fire.
At 3:30, Andaya, the head of Maui's emergency agency, sent a text: closing Lahaina Bypass road. Fire jump over to the roadway.
Police radio logs capture the speed of it. At 3:23, an officer reports blocking the bypass into Lahaina. At 3:52: Front Street at a standstill.
The wind had already knocked out cell towers. Power was out. Many people had no idea how close the fire was.
Alerts did go out. A road closure. Then, at 4:10, an evacuation order for one neighborhood at the top of town.
But when investigators later interviewed seventy-one residents, eighty-seven percent said they never received a single text alert.
At 4:24, someone reported fire near the banyan tree. That is more than a mile from where the morning fire began.
At the same minute, the first death was reported, on Mill Street. At 4:46, the fire crossed the highway into the heart of Lahaina.
Officers were breaking open locked gates so residents could escape. Embers were flying ahead of the flames, lighting roofs blocks away.
And the roads out of town were jammed.
A fallen utility pole blocked one direction of the highway. Traffic was turned away in the other. Survivors describe police cars and utility crews blocking roads.
The police chief later said officers never stopped anyone from leaving. Accounts still conflict.
But many survivors agree on one thing. The people who drove around the barricades lived.
Another said: the gridlock would have left us there when the firestorm came.
One survivor told reporters: we literally had minutes, and one wrong turn. We would all be dead right now.

title: THE OCEAN
lines: For many people, there was only one direction left.
Some sheltered behind the seawall. Others went into the water to escape the heat and the smoke, as the town burned behind them.
Around 5:45, the Coast Guard learned that people were in the ocean.
Boat crews from Station Maui spent the night searching the smoke. They pulled seventeen people from the water and helped forty more survivors ashore.
At 7:19 that evening, Andaya told state officials he believed only one business had been lost.
By then, much of Lahaina was gone.
The fire would not be fully contained for twenty-six days.

title: THE SILENT SIRENS
lines: Herman Andaya was not on Maui that afternoon. He was at a conference on Oʻahu.
At 4:03, as the fire was moving toward town, he texted: should I come home?
Hawaiʻi has one of the largest outdoor siren systems in the world. On Maui alone, there are eighty sirens.
On August eighth, not one of them was sounded.
A week later, a reporter asked Andaya if he regretted that decision. He answered: I do not.
He explained that people are trained to seek higher ground when a siren sounds. We just don't use sirens for fires, he said.
Had we sounded the siren that night, he said, we were afraid that people would have gone mauka, toward the mountain, and into the fire.
The next day, he resigned, citing health reasons.
The investigation that followed found the full story was worse.
Nobody had even discussed using the sirens. They had never been used for a wildfire, not even in 2018.
And of the five sirens around Lahaina, only two were listed as working. They relied on a cell network that was already failing.
Investigators concluded that a siren might not have told people what to do. But it might have given them one more warning.

title: THE WATER
lines: And then there was the water.
As firefighters pulled hoses into the streets, the hydrants began to lose pressure.
One Lahaina firefighter put it simply: there was just no water in the hydrants.
It wasn't that Lahaina had run out of water. The system was bleeding.
Inside every burning house, plastic pipes melted and broke open. Water poured out of burning homes all over town, and the pressure in the hydrants collapsed.
From the air, help was impossible. The gusts were too strong for helicopters to drop water.
On the ground, firefighters were fighting a firestorm, with almost nothing.

title: WHO IS RESPONSIBLE
lines: The answer that came back was not one person. It was a system.
Hawaiian Electric had no program to shut off power before dangerous winds. Its chief executive told Congress such shutoffs were not an appropriate fit for Hawaiʻi.
In October 2024, the official cause report ruled the fire accidental. Broken, re-energized power lines had started the morning fire. The afternoon fire was that same fire, rekindled.
The lead federal agent said of the firefighters: I do believe they did everything possible.
Hawaiian Electric said it deeply regretted that its operations contributed to the fire that ignited in the morning.
The state's independent investigation went further. It listed eighty-four findings, and concluded that no single factor caused the disaster.
The attorney general called it a wake-up call for the state and county governments.
Warnings that were never studied. A fire that came back after the crews had gone. Alerts that never arrived. Sirens nobody considered. Roads that clogged. Hydrants that ran dry.
As the head of the institute that led the investigation put it: the conditions that made this tragedy possible were years in the making.
In 2024, seven defendants, including the state, Maui County and Hawaiian Electric, agreed to a settlement of more than four billion dollars.
Hawaiian Electric now has a program to cut the power when dangerous winds arrive. It started in July 2024. The company calls it a last line of defense.

title: WHAT WAS LOST
lines: One hundred and two people died in the Lahaina fire.
The youngest was seven. The oldest was ninety-seven. Most were older; the median age was sixty-eight.
At least sixty-five of them were trying to get out. Some were found in their homes. Some in their cars. Some outdoors, in the streets they knew.
Eighty-two of them died in central Lahaina. Seven died at a single senior housing complex.
More than two thousand buildings were damaged or destroyed. Most of them were homes.
At one point, three hundred and eighty-eight people were listed as missing. The last victim died in March 2024, seven months after the fire.
Nearly eight thousand people spent months living in hotels.
Three years later, Lahaina is still rebuilding. By August 2026, a few hundred homes had been rebuilt. On historic Front Street, rebuilding had barely begun.
But in the old town square, the banyan tree is still standing.
Half of its branches died in the fire. The other half is growing back.
The Lahaina fire is often described as a natural disaster. A freak wind. A perfect storm.
But almost every part of it had been seen before.
The dry grass was on the hills for years. The 2018 fire burned right next door. The wind was forecast days in advance.
The sirens were on their poles. The fire was declared out. And the crews went home.
Lahaina did not burn because nobody could see the danger. It burned because so many small warnings were never put together.
And on August eighth, eighty sirens stayed silent.
